lessons.title: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
lessons.body: In cold storage, PPE is your first line of defence against frostbite, chemical burns, and physical injuries. You need insulated gloves, a thermal jacket, thermal trousers, and non-slip boots. For ammonia areas, keep a full-face respirator with ammonia cartridges, chemical splash goggles, and a face shield. Ear protection is essential because compressors and fans can exceed 85 decibels. Always check PPE before each shift: look for tears, cracks, or missing straps. In Africa, where heat outside can be 35Â°C and inside -25Â°C, layering is key. Wear moisture-wicking base layers, then fleece, then a windproof outer layer. Never wear loose clothing that can catch on machinery. For refrigerant handling, add cryogenic gloves and an apron. Store PPE in a clean, dry locker room. Replace worn items immediatelyâdon't wait for a purchase order. A simple rule: if you can see your skin through a glove, it's useless. Train every worker to inspect and don PPE in under two minutes. Keep a spare set for visitors. Remember, PPE only works if you wear it correctly: seal the respirator with a fit test, tighten boot laces, and fasten all zippers. In many African facilities, dust and humidity degrade gear quickly, so inspect weekly and replace every six months for gloves and filters. Document all inspections in a logbook. Your life depends on this gearâtreat it like your most important tool.

lessons.title: Ammonia and Refrigerant Leak Response
lessons.body: Ammonia is common in African cold stores because it's cheap and efficient, but it's deadly. You can smell it at 5 parts per million (ppm); at 300 ppm, it's immediately dangerous. If you smell ammonia, don't panic. First, hold your breath and walk upwind to fresh air. Never runârunning increases inhalation. Alert others by shouting 'Ammonia leak!' and activate the nearest alarm. If you're trained and have a full-face respirator with ammonia cartridges, you can shut the emergency valve, usually a red quarter-turn valve near the compressor. Otherwise, evacuate immediately. For other refrigerants like R-404A or R-134a, they're heavier than air and displace oxygen. If you feel dizzy, leave at once. Use a leak detector or soap bubbles to find leaksânever a lighter. Once safe, call your supervisor and the fire brigade if large. Treat anyone exposed: move to fresh air, flush eyes with water for 15 minutes, and seek medical help. For skin contact with liquid refrigerant, warm the area with lukewarm waterâdo not rub. In Africa, many facilities lack gas masks, so keep a 5kg bag of lime or baking soda to neutralise small ammonia spills. But never enter a confined space without a buddy and a rescue line. After any leak, ventilate the area with fans for at least 30 minutes before restarting. Document the incident and replace all filters. Practice a leak drill every three months. Speed saves lives: a 10-second delay can cause permanent lung damage.

lessons.title: Fire Prevention and Suppression
lessons.body: Cold storage fires often start from electrical faults, overheated compressors, or welding sparks. In Africa, many facilities use diesel generators, so keep fuel stored 10 metres away. Prevent fires by cleaning lint from condenser coils weekly, checking wiring for rodent damage, and never storing flammable chemicals like paint or solvents inside. Install smoke detectors and a fire alarm that can be heard over machinery noise. For suppression, use a dry powder or CO2 extinguisherânever water on electrical fires. Place extinguishers every 15 metres and check the pressure gauge monthly. A simple rule: PASSâPull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep. For small fires, aim at the base. If a fire is bigger than a wastebasket, evacuate and call the fire brigade. In cold rooms, fires can smoulder due to low oxygen, so always investigate burning smells. Train every worker to use an extinguisher once a year. Keep a sand bucket near welding areas. For ammonia fires, never use waterâit reacts violently. Use CO2 or dry chemical. If you see smoke, feel the door with the back of your hand. If hot, don't open. In many African settings, fire brigades may take 20 minutes, so your first response is critical. Have a fire blanket for small pan fires. After any fire, check for hidden embers in insulation. Replace all extinguishers that have been used, even partially. Keep a log of all inspections and drills. A fire drill every six months is mandatory.

lessons.title: Emergency Evacuation Plans
lessons.body: A cold storage facility has unique evacuation challenges: heavy doors, limited exits, and freezing temperatures. Your plan must be written, posted at every exit, and practiced. First, map all exitsâat least two per room, and keep them clear of pallets and boxes. Mark exits with glow-in-the-dark signs that work when power fails. Assign a floor warden for each shift. When the alarm sounds, stop work immediately, turn off machinery if safe, and walkâdon't runâto the nearest exit. In cold rooms, move quickly but carefully; icy floors cause falls. If you're trapped, use your phone or radio to call for help and bang on pipes. For ammonia leaks, evacuate upwind and uphill. For fires, stay low to avoid smoke. Once outside, go to the assembly pointâa painted circle or sign at least 50 metres from the building. The warden takes a headcount using a staff list. Never re-enter until the fire brigade or safety officer says it's safe. In Africa, where many workers speak different languages, use pictograms and simple words like 'Exit' and 'Assembly Point'. Practice evacuations every three months, including one at night. Time your drills: everyone should be out in under 3 minutes. Keep a whistle and torch on your person. If you have visitors, brief them on exits before entering. After any evacuation, review what went wrong and update the plan. A good plan is simple, practiced, and known by all.

lessons.title: Lockout/Tagout Procedures
lessons.body: Lockout/Tagout (LOTO) prevents machines from starting while you're repairing them. In cold storage, this applies to compressors, fans, conveyors, and electrical panels. The rule: every energy sourceâelectric, pneumatic, hydraulic, or thermalâmust be isolated. First, notify all affected workers that you're shutting down. Then, turn off the main disconnect switch. Apply your personal padlock and a tag with your name and date. Never use someone else's lock. For electrical panels, use a lockout hasp that holds multiple locks. For valves, use a gate valve lockout. Test the machine by trying to start itâif it doesn't move, it's safe. If it starts, stop and find another energy source. In Africa, many facilities have old equipment without standard disconnects, so use a chain and padlock through the breaker handle. Always keep the key with youânever leave it in the lock. When the job is done, remove your lock only after all workers are clear. Replace guards, then notify others before re-energising. Tagout alone is not enoughâtags can fall off. Always use a lock. Train every maintenance worker on LOTO before they touch any machine. Keep a LOTO kit with locks, tags, hasps, and a logbook. Inspect locks monthly for rust. A simple rule: if you didn't lock it, don't touch it. LOTO saves livesâover 100 workers die each year in Africa from unplanned machine start-ups. Don't be a statistic.

lessons.title: First Aid and CPR Basics
lessons.body: In cold storage, common injuries are cuts, frostbite, chemical burns, and cardiac arrest from electric shock or ammonia exposure. Your first aid kit must include sterile gauze, bandages, burn gel, eye wash, scissors, and a CPR mask. Check it monthly and replace expired items. For frostbite, move the person to a warm room (20-25Â°C). Do not rub the area. Soak in warm water (37-39Â°C) for 20-30 minutes. If blisters form, cover loosely. For chemical burns from ammonia, flush with water for at least 15 minutes. Remove contaminated clothing. For cuts, apply direct pressure with a clean cloth. For CPR, if someone is unresponsive and not breathing, call for help and start chest compressions: push hard and fast in the centre of the chest, at least 100-120 compressions per minute, 5-6 cm deep. Use an AED if available. In Africa, ambulances may take time, so you are the first responder. For electric shock, turn off power before touching the victim. For heat exhaustion (from working in hot outside areas), move to shade and give water. For hypothermia (from cold rooms), wrap in blankets and give warm drinks. Never give alcohol. Train at least two people per shift in first aid and CPR. Recertify every two years. Keep a written incident report. Practice scenarios monthly. Remember: your actions in the first 5 minutes can save a life. Stay calm, act fast, and never put yourself in danger.

quiz.q: What is the minimum number of exits required per cold storage room?
quiz.explanation: At least two exits are required to ensure evacuation if one is blocked.

quiz.q: At what concentration can you first smell ammonia?
quiz.explanation: Ammonia has a detectable odour at around 5 parts per million.

quiz.q: Which type of extinguisher should never be used on an electrical fire?
quiz.explanation: Water conducts electricity and can cause electrocution.

quiz.q: What does the acronym PASS stand for in fire extinguisher use?
quiz.explanation: PASS is the standard technique for using a fire extinguisher.

quiz.q: How often should you practice an emergency evacuation drill?
quiz.explanation: Regular drills every three months ensure readiness, including night drills.

quiz.q: What is the first step when you notice an ammonia leak?
options: B) Hold your breath and walk upwind
quiz.explanation: Holding your breath and moving upwind minimizes inhalation of toxic gas.

quiz.q: Which PPE is essential for ammonia response?
options: B) Full-face respirator with ammonia cartridges
quiz.explanation: Ammonia requires a full-face respirator with specific cartridges to protect eyes and lungs.

quiz.q: What is the correct water temperature for treating frostbite?
quiz.explanation: Warm water at 37-39Â°C thaws tissue without causing burns.

quiz.q: How deep should chest compressions be during CPR?
quiz.explanation: Compressions should be at least 5 cm deep for effective CPR.

quiz.q: What is the first thing you should do before repairing a machine?
quiz.explanation: Lockout/Tagout isolates all energy sources to prevent accidental start-up.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a sign of frostbite?
quiz.explanation: Red, hot skin indicates a burn or infection, not frostbite.

quiz.q: How often should you inspect your PPE?
quiz.explanation: PPE should be inspected before each use to ensure it is in good condition.

quiz.q: What should you do if a fire is larger than a wastebasket?
options: A) Try to put it out
B) Evacuate and call the fire brigade
D) Wait for it to burn out
quiz.explanation: Large fires require professional help; evacuate immediately.

quiz.q: Where should the assembly point be located?
options: B) At least 50 metres from the building
quiz.explanation: A safe distance prevents injury from explosions or toxic fumes.

quiz.q: What is the correct compression rate for CPR?
quiz.explanation: 100-120 compressions per minute is the recommended rate for adult CPR.

quiz.q: Which refrigerant is heavier than air and can displace oxygen?
quiz.explanation: R-404A is a common refrigerant that is heavier than air and can cause asphyxiation.

quiz.q: What should you never use to detect a refrigerant leak?
quiz.explanation: A lighter can ignite flammable refrigerants or cause an explosion.

quiz.q: How long should you flush an eye exposed to ammonia?
quiz.explanation: Flush with water for at least 15 minutes to remove all chemical residue.

quiz.q: What is the first step in LOTO?
quiz.explanation: Notification prevents accidental start-up by others.

quiz.q: Which item is NOT part of a first aid kit?
quiz.explanation: A lighter is not a first aid item and can be dangerous.

quiz.q: How often should you replace ammonia respirator cartridges?
quiz.explanation: Cartridges degrade over time; replace every six months or when damaged.

quiz.q: What should you do for a chemical burn from liquid refrigerant?
options: D) Cover with a tight bandage
quiz.explanation: Warming with lukewarm water helps thaw frozen tissue without further damage.

quiz.q: How often should you test smoke detectors?
quiz.explanation: Monthly testing ensures detectors are functional.

quiz.q: What is the maximum time for a full evacuation?
quiz.explanation: Aim for evacuation in under 3 minutes to ensure safety.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of hypothermia?
quiz.explanation: Shivering and confusion are early signs of hypothermia.

quiz.q: What should you do if you are trapped in a cold room?
options: B) Use phone or radio to call for help
quiz.explanation: Calling for help is the fastest way to get rescued.

quiz.q: How often should you recertify in first aid and CPR?
quiz.explanation: Certification typically expires after two years and must be renewed.

quiz.q: What is the correct action for a small ammonia spill?
options: A) Use water to wash it away
B) Neutralise with lime or baking soda
D) Use a fan to disperse it
quiz.explanation: Lime or baking soda neutralises ammonia safely.

quiz.q: Which PPE is needed for ear protection?
quiz.explanation: Earplugs or earmuffs reduce noise to safe levels below 85 dB.

quiz.q: What should you do before re-energising a machine after LOTO?
quiz.explanation: Notify all workers that the machine will be re-energised to prevent injury.
